planting.note: Start new plants from leaf cuttings or small tubers once indoor temperatures stay reliably above 65F; resume watering dormant tubers in early spring.

directions: This long-popular miniature hybrid, raised in the 1960s by crossing two dwarf Sinningia species, forms a tight rosette of rounded leaves topped by lavender, slipper-shaped flowers. Grow it in a small pot of airy, peat-free mix under bright, filtered light rather than sun, since direct rays scorch the fuzzy foliage. Keep humidity high and water from below or along the pot edge so the crown stays dry, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. After flowering the plant may die back to a small tuber; withhold water until fresh growth appears and resume a normal routine.

planting.note: Pot up rooted stolon plantlets in spring once nights stay above 60F; establish indoors or in a shaded, humid porch setting.

directions: Registered in the 1950s as a rare yellow-flowered sport within the usually red- or orange-blooming Episcia cupreata group, this cultivar carries bright green, crinkled leaves and sparse but striking buttery-gold flowers. Grow it in a hanging basket or wide shallow pot where its trailing stolons can spread and root freely, using a loose, humus-rich mix that drains fast. Provide warm temperatures, high humidity, and bright but indirect light, since the plant is grown as much for its glossy foliage mat as for its occasional blooms. Trim wandering stolons back to keep the planting full rather than straggly.

planting.note: Divide scaly rhizomes in spring and pot into fresh, well-drained mix as new shoots emerge.

directions: Bred in 1971 from two Kohleria species, this hybrid produces upright, softly hairy stems hung with tubular, speckled pink-and-white flowers over a long summer season. Give it bright, filtered light rather than full sun, since the fuzzy foliage scorches easily, and keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Pinch young growth to encourage branching and a fuller flowering habit, and expect the plant to die back to underground rhizomes in cool, short-day conditions. Repot or divide the rhizomes each spring to keep clumps vigorous and free-blooming.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in a warm, humid propagation box in spring before moving young plants to hanging containers.

directions: Native to Mexico and Honduras, this species carries noticeably thicker, more leathery leaves than the common hybrid goldfish plants, with bright orange-red flowers emerging along the stems in a stiffer, more upright habit than typical trailing Columnea. Grow it in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix and allow the surface to dry between thorough waterings, since the sturdy leaves store some moisture and resent constant wet soil. Place it where it receives bright, indirect light; stronger light than most Columnea tolerate, encourages the heaviest bloom. Because older stems become semi-woody, occasional pruning after flowering keeps the plant compact and encourages fresh flowering shoots.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem cuttings in a humid propagation tray in spring, then transplant to a hanging pot once rooted.

directions: A Brazilian native distinct from the more commonly grown Nematanthus gregarius, this species has small, glossy, waxy leaves that emerge coppery-red before darkening, paired with pouch-shaped golden-orange flowers that give the genus its goldfish-plant nickname. Grow it in dappled shade in a loose, bark-based mix, since harsher light can bleach the leaf color while deep shade reduces flowering. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and mist occasionally to mimic the humid understory conditions it grows in naturally. Its trailing stems make it well suited to a hanging basket on a shaded porch in warm climates.

planting.note: Divide offset rosettes or root leaf cuttings in spring, keeping new divisions shaded and humid until established.

directions: First described from limestone caves in southern China, this was the original species to carry the genus name Primulina before many former Chirita species were folded in alongside it, and it remains a distinct, low-growing rosette plant. Its soft green leaves release a faint tobacco-like scent when brushed or crushed, a quirk that sets it apart from its relatives. Grow it in deep, even shade with a mineral-rich, fast-draining mix, since in the wild it roots directly into limestone crevices with little organic matter. Keep humidity moderate to high and water sparingly, letting the mix dry slightly between waterings to avoid rot at the crown.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring under warm, bright-shade conditions; variegation is most stable in cuttings taken from well-lit stems.

directions: This variegated sport of the common trailing goldfish plant carries glossy leaves splashed in shades of green, cream, and sometimes pink, making it as much a foliage plant as a flowering one, alongside the usual inflated orange-red blooms. It needs noticeably brighter light than plain-leaved Nematanthus gregarius to hold its color pattern, since low light causes the variegation to fade back toward solid green. Let the thick, waxy leaves dry out somewhat between waterings, as they store moisture like a succulent, and avoid overwatering. Display it in a hanging basket on a bright but shaded porch, turning the pot occasionally for even growth.
